newsitem.title: JAPAN: Parties agree to end holding firm ban - party member.
newsitem.headline: Parties agree to end holding firm ban - party member.

text.p: Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and its allies reached an agreement on Tuesday to lift a decades-long ban on holding companies, a member of one of the parties said.

The three parties -- the LDP, the Social Democratic Party (SDP) and the small Sakigake party -- also agreed that the establishment of any holding company which would have total assets of 15 trillion yen or more would require prior government approval, Taku Yamasaki, chairman of the LDP's policy committee, told a news conference.

Under the agreement, any holding company that would have total assets of 300 billion yen or more would have to notify the Fair Trade Commission, Japan's anti-monopoly watchdog, of its establishment, he said.

A statement issued by three parties said that while Japan's anti-monopoly law had played a major role in helping develop the national economy, Japan now needed to carry out economic and financial reform.
The three parties had agreed to lift the 50-year-old ban to help diversify corporate management amid fierce international competition, it said.

An LDP member said on Monday that the agreement among the LDP and its two allies would enable the government to work out necessary changes to the anti-monopoly law and submit them to the current session of parliament by March 11.
Yamasaki said a bill to amend Japan's anti-monopoly law would likely take effect within a year.

He said 315 firms in Japan currently had assets exceeding 300 billion yen on a group basis, while even companies the size of telecom giant Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp (NTT) and Tokyo Electric Power Co Inc did not have assets exceeding 15 trillion yen.
Revision of the anti-monopoly law is also needed to allow implementation of a plan unveiled last year to restructure NTT into a collection of firms under a holding-company umbrella.

Yamasaki said the three parties had agreed that certain types of holding companies would be banned to avoid an excessive concentration of business strength and to avoid a rebirth of powerful conglomerates known as "zaibatsu".
Zaibatsu were banned by U.S. occupation forces after World War Two as Washington believed they had contributed to Japan's war effort.
Yamasaki said guidelines to define what types of holding companies would be prohibited would be worked out later.
He said the government must try hard to work out changes in finance-related laws to enable financial institutions to establish holding firms once the amended anti-monopoly law takes effect.

Yamasaki also said that the Japanese Trade Union Confederation and the Japan Federation of Employers' Associations had agreed to conclude talks within two years on the issue of labour-management negotiations once holding firms are established.
